title: Incident legacy handovers and rotation continuity playbook
author: Leah Morgan
body:
Summary:
This playbook defines how to perform structured incident handovers (legacy handovers), maintain rotation continuity across PTO/leave/handoffs, and ensure knowledge transfer so that ongoing incidents and operational contexts are preserved. It brings together process, templates, and automations used by Redwood Inference responder teams to avoid single points of failure during shift changes and long-running incidents.

Scope and objectives:
- Applies to all production-impacting incidents and any multi-hour degraded state (SLO impact > 10 minutes).
- Goals: preserve context, minimize time-to-recovery regressions during handoffs, ensure clear ownership, and enable rapid onboarding during rotations and game days.

Quick links and tooling (operational):
- PagerDuty service: PD: Redwood-Prod-Responder (pagerduty.com/teams/redwood-prod-responder)
- Status page: status.redwood.ai (API: POST https://status.redwood.ai/api/v1/incidents)
- Primary comms channel: #ops-bridge in Slack (pinned: runbook links, incident checklist)
- Postmortem template: /confluence/incident-postmortem-template
- Runbook storage: git repo infra/runbooks (branch: runbook-sync)

Incident lifecycle for handover (step-by-step):
1) Immediate triage (first 15 minutes): acknowledge, set bridge, identify impact and scope, assign preliminary roles.
2) Stabilize and document (15–60 minutes): capture hypothesis, mitigations attempted, current system state, and key artifacts (logs, traces, dumps).
3) Handover checkpoint (every shift or on role change): use the Handover Checklist (below). Prepare a 5-minute verbal summary + written status.
4) Continuity ownership: the oncoming responder becomes primary owner after the explicit ‘I accept’ on the bridge and in PagerDuty.
5) Release and follow-up: once resolved, triage follow-up actions, create RFCs for mitigations that require engineering work, and schedule a postmortem if impact > SLO threshold.

Handover checklist (required for any >30 minute incident or shift change):
- Incident ID and headline summary (1 line).
- Current severity and customer impact (S1/S2; affected regions, customer subsets).
- Time-synced timeline of major actions (timestamped bullets).
- Hypothesis and next diagnostic steps (top 3).
- Systems touched and relevant dashboards/queries (URLs).
- Mitigations in flight (exact commands/runbook steps) and rollback plan.
- Outstanding blockers (access, quota, external vendor waits).
- Expected next checkpoint time (default: 30 minutes).
- Name of proposed owner and backup.
- Location of artifacts: logs, core dumps, heap profiles, KV snapshots.

Roles and responsibilities (quick definitions):
- Incident Commander (IC): overall orchestration, coordinates stakeholders, decides severity escalation, authorizes customer communications.
- Bridge Operator: runs technical diagnostics, executes runbook steps, performs rollback actions.
- Communications Lead: drafts status page and customer messages, posts to channels, liaises with customer success.
- Service Owner: engineering owner for the affected service, responsible for root cause fixes and long-term mitigation tasks.
- Scribe: maintains the incident timeline and preserves artifacts for the postmortem.

Acceptance protocol for handover (verbal + written):
1) Oncoming person states: Name, role, and ‘I accept ownership for incident <ID>’.
2) Outgoing person confirms transfer by summarizing key open tasks and risks (1–2 bullets).
3) Both update PagerDuty incident with acceptance note and update the incident document in the bridge channel.

Escalation ladders and thresholds (examples):
- Latency SLO breach: P95 > 1500ms for 5 minutes -> escalate to IC.
- Error rate increase: 5xx rate > 3x baseline for 10 minutes -> immediate page and bridge.
- Provisioning capacity shortfall: queue growth > 30% sustained for 10 minutes -> alert on-call infra and IC.

Sample commands and diagnostics to include in handovers:
- curl checks: curl -sS https://example-service.internal/health | jq
- k8s: kubectl -n prod get pods -l app=service -o wide
- logs: tail -n 500 /var/log/service/worker.log | sed -n '1,200p'
- re-start cautiously: systemctl restart redwood-service (only with explicit approval)

On-call rotation continuity policies (practical):
- Shift length: primary on-call shifts are 12-hour blocks (07:00–19:00, 19:00–07:00 local). Either handover must occur at scheduled boundaries or immediate ad-hoc handover for active incidents.
- Overlap window: 15 minutes of planned overlap for shift turnover; for critical services, 30 minutes recommended.
- Long-running incidents: schedule a formal handover between ICs every 4 hours even if shifts align (to minimize fatigue and decision errors).
- PTO and leave: nominated backup must be confirmed 72 hours before shift; if not, on-call coordinator must reassign.
- Succession plan: team rotates primary -> secondary -> tertiary; secondary must have runbook familiarity and binder session quarterly.

Game day and simulation guidance (use-case driven):
- Cadence: quarterly service-level game days per critical service.
- Objectives: validate handover flows, test cross-team escalation, and exercise customer comms.
- Scenarios: silent SLO regression, cross-region failover, KV cache corruption with stale reads, and noisy neighbor-induced latency spike.
- Scoring rubric (example):
  - Detection effectiveness (0–5): how fast the incident was detected.
  - Handover quality (0–5): completeness of checklist and artifacts.
  - Communication clarity (0–5): status messages and customer notices.
  - Recovery correctness (0–5): appropriate mitigations and no regressions post-fix.
- After each game day: produce a short retro with 3 concrete action items assigned to owners and a due date.

Postmortem trigger and template (when to run):
- Trigger: any incident with customer impact > 30 minutes, any P1, or an incident that caused data loss.
- Template fields (must be filled): Title, Incident ID, Timeline (minute-level), Impact, Root cause hypothesis, Corrective actions (with owners & dates), Mitigation plan, Metrics regression and rebaseline, Lessons learned, Follow-up RFCs/PRs.

Customer communications and status page templates (examples):
- Short status update (internal / early):
  - Subject: [INC-<ID>] Early update — investigating elevated latency
  - Body: We are investigating elevated latency affecting a subset of API requests. Engineers are on a bridge and we will provide an update in 30 minutes. Impact: some requests may see slower responses (P95).
- Public status page template (example payload snippet):
  - Title: Elevated API latency
  - Impact: Customers in us-west may experience increased response times for text-generation endpoints.
  - Updates: 2027-02-10T14:12Z — Engineers identified a routing misconfiguration and are rolling back a recent network rule. Next update at 14:40Z.
- Customer-facing e-mail (for major incidents):
  - Subject: Service disruption affecting API responses — update
  - Body: Dear customer, We experienced an incident between 14:00–15:05 UTC that increased latency for some API calls. Root cause: config rollout that changed routing. We mitigated the issue by rolling back the rollout at 14:30 UTC. No data loss is expected. Next steps: we will run a change to improve rollout safety and share a timeline by 2027-02-15. If you have follow-up questions, reply to support@redwood.ai.

Evidence collection and artifact retention (must do during handover):
- Attach timeline.txt in the incident channel with minute-resolution bullets.
- Collect traces: save Jaeger trace IDs and export spans for the 30-minute window around the root cause.
- Store logs: move relevant logs to s3://redwood-incident-archive/<incident-id>/logs.zip.
- Preserve metrics: a CSV of the 10-minute buckets +/- 60 minutes around impact.

Handover automation recommendations (how to make it reliable):
- PagerDuty workflow: require acceptance action and auto-annotate incident with oncoming owner.
- Slack bot: slash command /handover create <incident-id> that scaffolds the checklist and pins the draft.
- Status API: make a small internal CLI (statusctl) to draft, preview, and post status updates with templated variables. Example: statusctl post --id INC-1234 --summary "Rolling back network rule" --impact "partial"

Runbook hygiene and ownership:
- Every runbook must declare: owner_email, last_review_date, and critical-test-month (month they are exercised).
- Runbook reviews: quarterly for P0/P1 services, biannual for P2/P3.
- Deprecation: mark runbooks stale if not exercised for 12 months; schedule owner to either refresh or retire.

Onboarding checklist for new on-call responders (minimum 3-day onboarding):
Day 0: read oncall handbook and runbook index, attend a shadow shift.
Day 1: run through a simulated incident (game-day mini) with a mentor.
Day 2: practice a handover and accept real low-severity pages under supervision.
Deliverable: a signed readiness note by the mentor in the onboarding doc.

Governance and review cadence:
- Monthly: incident trends review (SRE + service owners) to identify recurring handovers or knowledge gaps.
- Quarterly: game day for each critical service and runbook audit.
- Annual: rotation policy review and capacity planning tied to on-call burden metrics.

Appendix A — Minimal handover message template (1–2 lines, to be used in busy bridges):
- "INC-<ID> — Brief: <one-line impact>. Next action: <action-owner> will <step> by <time>. I accept: <oncoming-name>."

Appendix B — Example timeline snippet (format for scribe):
- 14:02 UTC — Alert fired: 5xx rate > 3x baseline
- 14:06 UTC — Bridge created: #ops-bridge-INC-1234
- 14:12 UTC — First mitigation: scaled webpool from 30 -> 45 nodes (rollback pending)
- 14:26 UTC — Root cause suspected: config rollout X

Related pages (recommended reads):
- /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-postmortem-template
- /confluence/eng-sre/availability-classification-and-restoration-sop

Owner and contact:
- Document owner: Leah Morgan (leah.morgan@redwood.ai)
- On-call coordinator: Priya Shah (priya.shah@redwood.ai)

Change log:
- 2026-11-05: Created (Leah Morgan)
- 2027-02-10: Added automated handover suggestions and sample statusctl CLI (Leah Morgan)

This playbook is intentionally prescriptive where handovers are involved and flexible elsewhere; teams should adopt the handover checklist verbatim for any incident >30 minutes.
